messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi had always been a proud man, taking care in his work as a hairdresser and striving to provide for his wife. But it was on a typical Wednesday evening, after closing up his shop, that his life took a drastic turn. As he walked home, lost in thought, he was suddenly grabbed from behind and mugged by two men. The event was over quickly, but the images of those few moments - the feel of hands grasping at his pockets, the smell of stale beer on one of the attacker's breath - seared themselves into Kofi's mind like a branding iron. In the weeks that followed, Kofi found himself increasingly withdrawn, unable to shake the feeling of vulnerability that lingered long after the mugging. When customers came into his shop, he would catch himself watching them warily, expecting another attack at any moment - and if they happened to act suspiciously, or even just made an offhand comment about his work, Kofi's mind would instantly flash back to those terrifying moments on the street. He'd try to push the thoughts away, but like a film reel stuck on repeat, the images of the mugging played over in his head - vivid pictures that he couldn't find words to describe. As these triggers took hold, Kofi began to turn inward, replaying every moment of the event and wondering what he could have done differently. He'd berate himself for walking alone at night, for not fighting back harder, or simply for being a target in the first place - dwelling on his perceived shortcomings with an intensity that bordered on obsession. His self-blame rumination became so all-consuming that Kofi started to avoid social interactions altogether, afraid of being criticised or corrected by others and further eroding what little confidence he had left. But even as Kofi tried to suppress these thoughts, they continued to resurface - triggered anew each time someone walked into his shop with a whiff of alcohol on their breath. And so the cycle would begin again: memories of the mugging flooding back, followed by recriminations and self-doubt, all combining to make Kofi feel like he was losing himself in an endless loop of fear and regret. Kofi's wife grew concerned as her once-vibrant husband became increasingly isolated - barely leaving their apartment except for work, where his usual charm had given way to sullen withdrawal. When she finally convinced him to seek help, it wasn't the memories themselves that Kofi feared most, but rather the crippling self-doubt and fear of being attacked again that now controlled his every waking moment. As he sat in the therapist's office, fidgeting nervously with his hands, Kofi confided that what brought him here was not just the memories or even the triggers themselves - but the crushing feeling of being trapped by his own mind. And though it took a quiet courage for him to do so, he whispered the simple truth: "I don't know who I am anymore."
